title: Rest isn't failure
hookLine: the World Health Organization lists burnout as a workplace phenomenon (2019)

cards: Burnout can sound like a personal weakness, something whispered about a colleague who couldn't keep up.
Then the World Health Organization put it in its international classification of diseases, the big reference doctors use to name what they see. It isn't listed there as an illness.
It's listed as a phenomenon of work: something that happens to people because of how they work. That wording moves the question. Not what's wrong with you, but what's been happening to you.

teach.b: First, the description. The World Health Organization describes burnout as coming from chronic stress at work that hasn't been successfully managed.
It names three marks: feeling depleted or exhausted; growing mental distance from your job, or feeling negative and cynical about it; and a sense that you're getting less done.
It doesn't call burnout laziness, or a lack of faith, or a flaw in character. Second, an old story that fits.
In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Elijah, after a great contest and a death threat, runs into the wilderness, sits under a tree and asks to die. What happens next is not a lecture. He sleeps.
An angel touches him and says, "Arise and eat." There's bread and water.
He sleeps again, and eats again. Only after that does the journey go on. The first answer to his despair is rest and food.
Third, a teacher who called a halt. In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus's followers come back so busy that, the text says, they had no time even to eat.
And he tells them, "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." In that story, stepping away is not abandoning the work. It's part of it.
Fourth, what this means on a Tuesday. If you are worn down to nothing, rest isn't the opposite of doing well. It may be what lets anything else happen.

teach.h: REST LETS THE WORK GO ON.
teach.b: And if burnout is a phenomenon of work, the fix may also need to change the work, not only the worker.
Rest is where that thinking can start.

how: People recovering from burnout often combine real breaks with changes to the work itself; some religious communities also keep regular times of rest and retreat.

o: exhaustion and distance from chronic, unmanaged work stress
a weakness of character in people who can't keep up
a medical illness doctors treat with a set course of rest

games.q: who said or did what — tap the pairs.
p: burnout is a phenomenon of work
slept under a tree in the wilderness

s: the WHO lists burnout as a phenomenon of work, not as an illness
it describes it as coming from chronic workplace stress that hasn't been successfully managed.
in the story, the angel scolds Elijah for despairing
the angel brings bread and water and lets him sleep; rest and food come first.
in Mark, Jesus tells his followers to keep working because so many people are coming
he tells them to come apart and rest a while.

games.q: Elijah has run into the wilderness, sat under a tree and asked to die. you're the angel. what do you do first?
o: give him a speech about courage.
let him sleep, then wake him with bread and water.
send him straight back to work.
games.why: the angel touches him and says arise and eat. he eats, sleeps again, eats again, and only then goes on.

practice: For these two minutes you're off duty: let your shoulders drop and your hands go loose, close your eyes if you can, and breathe out a little longer than you breathe in.

If a task comes to mind, picture setting it down on a table beside you; it'll still be there later. You don't have to achieve anything, not even a good meditation; just rest, the way Elijah slept under the tree.

wordCard.voice: Burnout. The World Health Organization's name for what chronic, unmanaged stress at work does to a person. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: arise and eat. Rest is part of the work, not a failure at it. Day nine hundred nine.

sources.q: Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while
